transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?

Well, hello, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I appreciate you taking the time. I wasn't entirely sure if I should even make an appointment, to be honest, but my wife really pushed me to come in. We've been married a long time, and she's usually the one who handles all the family logistics, which I'm very grateful for, but lately it's just been causing a lot of friction between us. 

What really brought me in is... well, it's this thing that keeps happening when she talks to me. For example, she's been helping out my cousin lately. He's been needing some help getting around, so she'll sit down with me to go over his schedule. She'll be telling me all about his appointments, or who is giving him rides on what day, just trying to keep me in the loop. And I swear to you, I am looking right at her. I'm sitting there, making eye contact, nodding along, trying my absolute best to be a supportive husband and pay attention. 

But then, maybe a minute later, she'll ask me a question about it, or I'll just suddenly realize on my own... I didn't actually take in half of what she just said. It's like the words just hit a brick wall and bounced off. And it frustrates her to no end, which I completely understand, because to her it looks like I just don't care or I'm ignoring her on purpose. But I'm really not! I'm sitting right there, looking right into her eyes. It's just incredibly frustrating, and honestly a bit embarrassing at my age, to not be able to just absorb what someone is saying to my face. So, she finally said enough is enough, you need to go talk to someone about this.

Besides having trouble remembering what your wife tells you, have you noticed any other changes in your thinking or memory? For example, do you have trouble finding words, or do you forget things you used to remember easily, like where you put things or appointments?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask about finding words, because I don't really have trouble with that, thankfully. I can still talk your ear off, as my wife would gladly tell you. But as for forgetting where I put things... oh, boy. Yes. That happens all the time. It's actually become a bit of a running joke, though I don't think my wife finds it very funny anymore. 

It’s just... I’m always putting things down. Just setting them down wherever I happen to be standing. My keys, for instance. I'll come in the door, and instead of putting them on the hook right there in the entryway like a normal person, I'll walk into the kitchen, maybe open the fridge, and just set the keys on the counter. Or I'll have these receipts from the catering business we used to run—we're retired now, but we still help out with some local events, you know, just to stay busy—and I'll set those down on the dining room table, or maybe the coffee table, and then poof, they're gone. 

My phone is another one. I'll have it in my hand, and then I'll go out to the garden—I love working in the garden, it's very peaceful, I grow tomatoes and some squash—and I'll take my garden clippers out there. And then I'll come back inside, and I won't have my phone, and I won't have the clippers. And then I have to spend, I don't know, ten, sometimes fifteen minutes just wandering around the house, retracing my steps, trying to figure out where I left them. I'll look in the bathroom, I'll look on the porch. It's exhausting, really. And it's not like I'm forgetting what a phone is, or what keys do, it's just... I set them down, and my brain just deletes the memory of doing it the second it happens.
Over what period of time have you noticed these memory problems developing? Did they start suddenly, or have they been gradually getting worse over weeks, months, or years?

Well, you know, it's interesting you ask about the timeline, because my wife and I were just talking about this the other day. We were sitting on the porch—it was a beautiful evening, actually, just perfect weather for sitting out—and she was saying how much worse it seems to have gotten lately. And she's right, she really is. 

I mean, I've always been a little scatterbrained, I suppose. Even back when we were running the catering business, I'd misplace an invoice here or there, or forget to call a vendor back right away. But it was manageable, you know? We had systems in place. But this... this level of just completely blanking on things, and losing my phone three times a day, it really hasn't always been this bad. 

If I really sit down and think about it, I'd say it's been noticeably harder for about... oh, eleven months now. Yes, right around eleven months. And I know exactly why, too, because that's when my cousin moved in with us. He had that terrible surgery—a knee replacement, actually, and it got infected, it was a whole ordeal, poor guy was in the hospital for a week—and he just couldn't manage the stairs at his place. So, of course, we took him in. Family is family, you know? We have the guest room downstairs, so it made perfect sense. 

But having him there... it just added this whole new layer of things to keep track of. Suddenly there are physical therapy appointments, and medication schedules, and dietary restrictions, and nurses coming in and out. And my wife, bless her heart, she handles the lion's share of it, but she needs me to be present and help out, and that's when I really started noticing that my brain just wasn't holding onto the information. It's like the moment he moved in, the circuits just overloaded. So yes, it's been about eleven months of this really frustrating, everyday forgetfulness, right since he came to stay with us.
Have you noticed any changes in how you move around, such as tremors in your hands, stiffness in your muscles, or slowness in your movements?

Tremors? Oh, no, no. Goodness, no. My hands are as steady as they’ve ever been. I mean, you have to have steady hands in the catering business, you know, for the plating and all the delicate work with the hors d'oeuvres, and I guess I never really lost that touch. Just this morning, actually, I was out in the garden—I think I mentioned my tomatoes earlier, didn't I? Well, I was out there tying them up to the stakes, which takes a fair bit of dexterity, threading the little pieces of twine and making sure you don't snap the stems, and I didn't have a bit of shaking. 

And as for being stiff or slow... well, I mean, I'm fifty-nine, so I'm not exactly going to be running marathons or doing cartwheels in the living room anytime soon, but I get around just fine. Honestly, I'm probably the most nimble one in the house right now, what with my cousin and his bad knee. He's the one who's slow, poor guy. It takes him ten minutes just to get from the guest room to the kitchen table with his walker. But me? No, I'm up and down the stairs all day, carrying his laundry, hauling forty-pound bags of potting soil out back for the squash beds... I feel pretty good physically, all things considered. My joints are fine, my muscles do what I tell them to. It's really just the, you know, the mental filing cabinet that seems to be spilling everything all over the floor. But physically, no, no changes at all.
Besides your cousin moving in, have you had any recent illnesses, infections, high fevers, hospitalizations, or have you started any new medications in the past year or so?

Well, let me think about that. Illnesses... no, not really. I mean, I had a bit of a sniffle back in January, or maybe it was February, right around the time we got that big snowstorm that knocked out the power for a few hours. But it was just a regular cold, nothing serious. Certainly no high fevers or anything that would put me in the hospital. I haven't been in a hospital as a patient since... gosh, since I had my tonsils out when I was twelve. 

And as for new medications, no, nothing new there either. I take my daily multivitamin, and a little something for my cholesterol—my doctor put me on that about five years ago, said my numbers were just creeping up a bit, probably from all those years tasting the rich foods we made for the catering business, you know how it is. But I haven't started anything new recently. My cousin, on the other hand, well, his medication list is a mile long since the surgery. He's got the antibiotics, the painkillers, the blood thinners... it's a full-time job just keeping track of his pill organizer. We had to get one of those big ones with the morning, noon, evening, and bedtime slots. But for me? No, my routine is exactly the same as it's always been. Just the vitamin and the cholesterol pill, and I've been pretty healthy overall, thankfully. So no, no big medical events or new prescriptions for me.

Over these past eleven months, have you noticed any changes in your mood or how you feel emotionally? For instance, do you feel more down, sad, or hopeless than you used to, or do things that you normally enjoy—like working in your garden—feel less enjoyable or interesting to you?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I wouldn't say I feel sad or down, no. It's funny you mention the garden, actually, because that's still my absolute favorite place to be. I was just telling my wife yesterday, when I was out there pulling weeds from the zucchini patch—and let me tell you, those weeds have been relentless this year with all the rain we've been getting, it's like a jungle out there if you turn your back for two days—but I was telling her that being out there, with my hands in the dirt, it's just as peaceful as it ever was. I still love it just as much. 

I guess... well, if anything, I just feel frustrated. Really, deeply frustrated with myself. It’s like, I want to do things, I want to help my wife with my cousin, I want to keep the house running smoothly, but I just keep dropping the ball. Like last week, I was supposed to pick up a special sort of padded cushion for his wheelchair from the medical supply store across town. I had it written down on a sticky note, stuck it right to the dashboard of the car. And I drove all the way out there, stopped at the hardware store next door to look at some new hoses for the garden, spent twenty minutes chatting with the clerk about water pressure, drove all the way back home, and completely forgot the cushion. I had to turn right around and go back. 

So it’s not that I’m hopeless or depressed, or that I don't care about things anymore. It’s just this constant, nagging annoyance that my brain isn't cooperating. It makes me feel a bit foolish, honestly, like I'm letting everyone down because I can't hold a simple instruction in my head for an hour. But emotionally, as far as being sad or losing interest in my hobbies... no, nothing like that. I still enjoy my gardening, I still enjoy a good meal, I still enjoy sitting on the porch with my wife. I just wish I could remember where I put my pruning shears half the time.

Has your primary care doctor done any recent blood work or other tests in the past year? If so, did they find anything abnormal, or have you had any recent visits with your doctor where they checked on your overall health?

Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I actually did see Dr. Henderson—he's been my primary care doctor for, gosh, it must be fifteen years now, ever since Dr. Miller retired and closed up his practice over on Elm Street. Anyway, I saw Dr. Henderson back in, let me think... it was right before Thanksgiving, because I remember we were talking about whether I should deep fry the turkey or stick to the traditional oven roasting. I used to do a lot of deep frying back in the catering days, but it's such a hassle with the peanut oil and the cleanup. 

But yes, I went in for my annual physical. He always does the whole workup, you know, listens to the heart, checks the reflexes, all of that. And he did send me down to the lab for blood work. I always hate that part, not because of the needle, mind you, but because you have to sit in that waiting room with the terrible fluorescent lighting and those outdated magazines. I think I read an article about decorating for Christmas in 2018 while I was waiting. 

But anyway, they took three vials, I think it was. Checked the cholesterol again, checked the blood sugar, the thyroid, all the standard things they look at when you're knocking on the door of sixty. And everything came back completely normal. He called me a few days later—well, his nurse, Brenda, called me. She's a sweetheart, always remembers to ask about my garden. She said everything looked great. The cholesterol was holding steady right where it should be with the medication, and my blood pressure was perfect, which honestly surprised me a little bit given how stressful it's been getting the house ready for my cousin to move in. But no, no abnormal tests, no strange results. Physically speaking, Dr. Henderson said I was in excellent shape for my age. Which, again, just makes it all the more baffling why I can't seem to remember to turn off the sprinkler system until the yard is practically a swamp. But as far as the blood work goes, clean as a whistle.

You mentioned your memory problems started about eleven months ago when your cousin moved in. Have these memory and concentration problems been getting steadily worse over these eleven months, or do they come and go—like some days are better than others, or some times of day are worse than other times?

Well, you know, I’ve actually asked myself that exact same question. My wife brought it up just the other week when we were sitting on the porch after dinner. She said to me, "Do you think this is getting worse?" And I had to really stop and think about it. Because, you know, when you’re in the thick of it, day in and day out, it’s hard to see the forest for the trees, as they say. You just sort of get used to your own stumbles.

At first, I thought, well, maybe it’s worse in the mornings. Because mornings are quite a production around here now. We get up, I get the coffee going—I still use that old French press I bought back in the late nineties, makes the absolute best cup, even if it is a bit of a hassle to clean out all those wet grounds—and then we have to get my cousin situated, get his breakfast sorted, make sure he’s comfortable in his chair for the day. So I thought, maybe my brain is just foggy before I've had my second cup of coffee and the house settles down. 

But then, just last Tuesday, I had a perfectly clear morning, got everything done without a hitch, and then right around two o'clock in the afternoon, I completely forgot why I walked into the garage. I stood there staring at the lawnmower for five solid minutes before I realized I was supposed to be getting the WD-40 for a squeaky hinge on the back screen door. And then sometimes it happens right after dinner! 

So, it doesn't really seem to matter what time of day it is, or if I'm tired or rested. And as for getting steadily worse... I don't know, I really don't think so. It feels like it’s just sort of... been exactly this way ever since the whole upheaval started eleven months ago. It doesn't feel like a downhill slide, thank goodness, which is a relief, but it doesn't really feel like it comes and goes in any predictable way, either. It’s just this constant, unpredictable thing. Some days I might drop the ball twice, some days I might drop it four times, but there’s no real rhyme or reason to it that I can figure out. I'm just consistently inconsistent now, I suppose you could say.

When you're walking around the house or outside in the garden, have you noticed any change in how you swing your arms, or do you ever feel like you're moving a bit more slowly or stiffly than you used to, even if you don't feel like you're having trouble getting around?

Well, no, I can't say that I have. My arms swing just like they always have, as far as I know. I mean, I don't exactly watch myself walk in a mirror, but I haven't felt any stiffness or anything like that. 

Actually, speaking of moving around, I was out in the yard just yesterday morning—well, wait, maybe it was the afternoon, right after lunch because I remember I had just finished a rather messy turkey and swiss sandwich—and I was carrying these big bags of mulch. Cypress mulch, you know, because I've found it keeps the bugs away much better than the pine bark, and it holds the moisture nicely during the August heat. Anyway, I was hauling them all the way from the driveway, around the side of the house, past those rhododendrons that are finally starting to bloom after looking completely dead all winter, and all the way back to the raised beds. If I was stiff or moving slow, I definitely wouldn't be able to lug forty-pound bags of mulch around like that! 

And as for the arm swinging, well, when I go for my walk down to the mailbox—we live on a bit of a flag lot, so the driveway is quite long, it's a good quarter-mile round trip just to get the daily post—I just walk my normal pace. I haven't noticed my arms doing anything peculiar, and my wife hasn't said anything about it either. And believe me, she would absolutely mention it if I was walking like a robot or shuffling along. She notices everything. Just last week, she noticed I had put my shirt on inside out before I even made it into the kitchen for breakfast. 

But physically, no, my joints and muscles feel pretty good for a guy knocking on sixty's door. Sure, maybe my knees crack a little bit when I squat down to pull a stubborn dandelion, but there's no real slowness or stiffness like you're talking about. I feel perfectly fine in that department, moving just as smoothly as I did a decade ago. It's just the memory that's giving me grief!
Have you noticed any difficulty with fine motor tasks, like buttoning your shirt, writing, or eating with utensils? Or do things that require precision seem to take you longer than they used to?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I haven't noticed any trouble with my hands or anything like that. It's funny you mention buttoning shirts, though, because I actually just bought a whole new set of those flannel shirts from L.L. Bean—you know the ones, the really thick, warm ones? I got a red and black plaid, a blue one, and this sort of forest green one that my wife says brings out my eyes, which is nice of her to say after all these years. Anyway, those shirts have the tiniest little buttons on the collar, the ones that hold the collar points down? And I manage those just fine every single morning. I don't fumble with them or anything. 

And as for writing, well, I still write out all our bills by hand. I know everyone does it online now, and my son keeps telling me I need to set up automatic payments, but I just prefer the physical act of writing the check, balancing the checkbook. I use this old Parker fountain pen that my grandfather gave me when I graduated high school. It's a beautiful pen, silver with this intricate crosshatch pattern on it, and it writes so smoothly. But you have to have a pretty steady hand to use a fountain pen without making a mess, especially when you're filling the ink converter from the bottle. I use this lovely midnight blue ink, and I've never spilled a drop or smudged a check. My handwriting is just as neat as it was when I was thirty. 

And eating... no problems there either. In fact, just last night we had spaghetti and meatballs, and I was twirling the pasta on my fork against the spoon, just the way they do it in Italy—or at least, the way they do it in the movies about Italy. No trouble at all. I can still use chopsticks, too, when we order from that little Thai place down the street, the one that makes the incredible Pad See Ew. So, no, my hands are working just fine. It's really just the forgetfulness, like walking into a room and having absolutely no idea why I went in there, or misplacing my glasses when they're sitting right on top of my head. But physically, my hands and fingers are doing exactly what I tell them to do, when I tell them to do it.
Has your wife or anyone else mentioned that your face seems less expressive than it used to be, or that you're blinking less often? Sometimes people don't notice these changes in themselves.

Less expressive? Oh, goodness, no. No, I don't think so at all. Like I was saying earlier about the inside-out shirt, my wife really doesn't miss a trick. If I were walking around staring blankly or not blinking, she would have sat me down and had a whole serious conversation about it by now. She's very observant like that. 

Actually, she always tells me that I'm absolutely terrible at playing cards because my face is like an open book and gives everything away. We used to play cards on Friday nights with our neighbors, the Hendersons—well, we haven't done it quite as much since my cousin moved in, because the evenings can be a bit unpredictable now, but we still try to get a game of Hearts or Spades going every now and then on the patio. And whenever I get a terrible hand, apparently my eyebrows shoot right up into my hairline, and I get this very specific sort of grimace. Bob Henderson always bids high when I get that look because he knows for a fact I've got absolutely nothing to play. I just can't hide what I'm thinking, it's all right there on my face. 

And as for the blinking thing, that's an interesting question, but no. Honestly, with the pollen this year, I feel like I'm blinking more than usual, if anything! We have all those massive oak trees lining the back property line, and they just coat absolutely everything in this fine yellow dust from about March straight through to May. It covers the patio furniture, the cars, everything. And it gets right in your eyes if the wind blows the wrong way. I'm constantly blinking and rubbing my eyes when I'm out checking the mail or messing with that cypress mulch I was telling you about. I even had to buy some of those little saline drops from the pharmacy last week just to flush my eyes out in the afternoons. 

So no, definitely not blinking less, and definitely not losing any expressions. I still smile, I frown, I look completely bewildered when I walk into the kitchen and forget why I'm standing in front of the open refrigerator... the expressions themselves are all still there in full force, believe me!

Have you been seeing, hearing, or experiencing anything that doesn't seem real—like seeing things that aren't there, or hearing voices or sounds that others don't hear? This can sometimes happen even just in the corner of your eye or for just a moment.

Seeing things? Hearing voices? Oh, goodness, no. No, nothing like that at all. My mind might be a sieve when it comes to where I put the television remote, but I'm definitely not hallucinating. I mean, the closest I've come to seeing something that wasn't there was last Tuesday—or maybe it was Wednesday, because it was raining, and it usually rains on Wednesdays here, it seems—when I thought I saw the neighbor's cat, Barnaby, sneaking into our garage. He's this massive, fluffy orange tabby, very mischievous, always trying to get into the trash cans. But when I went out there with a broom to shoo him away, it turned out to just be a crumpled-up paper bag from the grocery store that had blown in when the door was open. 

But that's just a trick of the light, you know? Just my eyes playing tricks on me in the shadows. Not a real hallucination or anything like what you're talking about. I certainly haven't been hearing voices or anything spooky. It's funny you mention hearing things, though, because my hearing is actually quite sharp. Too sharp, sometimes. Like I was saying about my cousin moving in, he has this habit of leaving the television on in the guest room at all hours. He falls asleep with it on, and even with the door closed and the volume turned down, I can still hear that low murmur of the late-night infomercials through the wall. It drives me absolutely up the wall when I'm trying to sleep. I have to use those little foam earplugs, the orange ones you roll up between your fingers before you put them in? They work wonders, but they do make your ears a bit itchy if you wear them too many nights in a row. 

But no, to answer your question, no voices, no visions, nothing out of the ordinary. Just the usual everyday sounds of the house settling, the wind in those oak trees, and the occasional infomercial drifting down the hallway. My reality is very firmly grounded, doctor, I promise you that. It's just my short-term memory that seems to have taken a vacation without me!

Has anyone mentioned that you seem to move more slowly than you used to, or that it takes you longer to do everyday tasks like getting dressed or preparing a meal, even though you don't feel like anything is wrong with your muscles?

Move slowly? Oh, no, definitely not. If anything, my wife is always telling me I need to slow down, especially when we're walking through the grocery store. I'll be three aisles over looking at the canned tomatoes before she's even finished picking out the apples. I've always had a pretty brisk walking pace, and that certainly hasn't changed. 

And as for getting dressed or making meals, no, I'm still quick as a whip with all of that. Like I mentioned with those flannel shirts earlier, I'm up and dressed and buttoned up in five minutes flat every morning. I actually handle the breakfast routine in our house, have for a few years now. I'm usually up around six-thirty, usually before the alarm even bothers to go off, and I head straight down to the kitchen. I've got this whole system figured out. I use a French press for the coffee, which takes exactly four minutes to steep, and in those four minutes, I'm practically a blur—getting the mugs out, putting the sourdough bread in the toaster, getting the butter out of the fridge so it softens up, cracking the eggs. I do two over-easy for myself and scrambled for my wife. I move around that kitchen like a short-order cook at a busy diner! 

Now, I will say, sometimes a task might take me a little longer from start to finish than it ought to, but that is absolutely not because my body is moving slowly. It's just because I get sidetracked along the way! Like just the other day, I went into the kitchen to make a turkey sandwich for lunch. I got the bread out, went to the fridge for the deli meat, noticed the water pitcher was completely empty, started filling that up at the sink, realized it needed a new filter, went to the pantry to find the replacement filters, and the next thing I know I'm organizing the canned soups by alphabetical order and the bread is just sitting out on the counter getting stale. So, sure, the whole lunch process took me forty-five minutes instead of five, but the physical movements? The walking, the reaching, the opening jars? All perfectly normal, perfectly up to speed. No physical slowness there whatsoever.
Have there been any times when you felt confused about where you were, or what day it was, or had trouble understanding what was going on around you—even if just for a few minutes?

Confused about where I am? Oh, no, no. Definitely not. I always know exactly where I am. Now, I might walk into the living room and completely forget *why* I went in there—just like I was saying before with the refrigerator, I'll just stand there staring at the coffee table wondering if I came in for my reading glasses, or the newspaper, or maybe to water the fern—but I certainly know I'm in my own living room! I've never looked around and not recognized my surroundings or felt lost. That would be quite frightening, I imagine. But no, nothing like that for me. 

As for what day it is... well, I will admit, since I'm not working these days, the week can sort of blend together just a little bit. When you don't have a time clock to punch or a morning commute to worry about, a Tuesday can feel an awful lot like a Thursday, you know? But it's not a genuine, deep confusion, it's just... well, it's just the reality of having a wide-open schedule. Plus, my wife keeps a big dry-erase calendar right on the side of the fridge. She has it completely color-coded, too, because like I said, she is incredibly organized. She uses a blue marker for our appointments, red for when the grandkids are coming over, and green for the yard waste pickup. The yard waste is every other Monday, which is actually a bit of a nuisance to keep track of, because if you miss it, those big brown paper bags of lawn clippings just sit out by the curb getting soggy if it rains, and then the bottom falls out when the sanitation guys try to lift them. So I have to stay on top of that. But anyway, if I ever have a momentary lapse of "is today Wednesday or Thursday," I just glance at the fridge. I'm never actually lost in time or disoriented. 

And as far as understanding what's going on around me... no, I'm fully present. I understand exactly what's happening. Sometimes I might be paying attention to the *wrong* thing, sure—like if my wife is trying to tell me about her sister's upcoming visit and I get completely distracted watching a blue jay at the bird feeder outside the window—but I understand the situation perfectly well. I'm just a bit scatterbrained, that's all. But I am completely grounded in reality. I know exactly who I am, where I am, and what year it is, I can promise you that.

You mentioned that sometimes your memory seems better or worse at different times. Have you ever had periods where you felt like you weren't quite as aware or alert as usual—like your mind felt foggy or cloudy, or like you were having trouble focusing even when you were trying your hardest? Did that ever come on suddenly, or did it seem to shift throughout the day?

Foggy or cloudy? Oh, no, I wouldn't use those words at all. No, my mind isn't foggy. If anything, it's the exact opposite—it's almost too clear, just taking in way too many things at once! I don't ever get these sudden shifts where I'm not aware of things or where my consciousness just sort of dims out. I'm always very alert. 

Like, just yesterday afternoon, for example. I was out on the back patio trying to read this new biography of Ulysses S. Grant. Fascinating man, by the way, the way he handled the logistics of the Vicksburg campaign is just incredible, though the book itself is a bit dry in the early chapters about his childhood in Ohio. But anyway, I was sitting out there, fully awake, fully alert. I had my reading glasses on, I had a glass of iced tea—unsweetened, because my primary care doctor told me I need to start watching my sugar intake, which is a whole other ordeal because I do love a good slice of cherry pie, especially the kind they sell at the bakery down on Main Street—but I was sitting there, trying my absolute hardest to focus on the page. 

Did my mind get foggy? No, not at all. I didn't lose awareness of my surroundings. What actually happened was I became incredibly aware of a cardinal landing on the fence, and then I noticed a hairline crack in the patio concrete that I really need to fill before winter sets in and the ice makes it worse, and then I spent twenty minutes trying to remember if I had any of that polyurethane concrete sealant left in the shed from when I patched the driveway last summer. 

So, you see, I wasn't cloudy or less alert. I didn't have a sudden drop in my awareness or anything concerning like that. I'm always sharp and awake, right from the minute I have that French press coffee I told you about until I finally put my head on the pillow at night. It's just that my focus doesn't always stay where I want it to stay. But the engine is always running, you know? There's no fog on the windshield... I'm just, well, I'm just looking out the side windows instead of straight ahead at the road. So no, to answer your question, no sudden shifts or cloudy periods whatsoever. I'm always completely switched on.

When you're doing tasks like tying up your tomato plants or writing with that fountain pen, have you noticed that your movements feel smaller or less expansive than they used to be—like you're not moving your arm as far, or your handwriting is getting a bit smaller, even though you're not trying to do that?

Smaller movements? Oh, absolutely not. No, my handwriting is just as big and bold as it’s always been. I actually have a very distinct signature, lots of big, sweeping loops. Like you mentioned with the fountain pen—I use a medium nib on that one. It’s a vintage Parker I picked up at an estate sale maybe five years ago. Or was it six? No, five, because it was the same summer we finally got around to repainting the back deck. But anyway, I use this beautiful midnight blue ink, and the thing about a medium nib is that if you write too small, the letters just bleed together into a giant puddle, especially if you're just using standard grocery list paper instead of the thick, heavy-stock stuff. So I have to write fairly large, and I always do. No shrinking letters whatsoever. My wife always jokes that I take up three whole lines on the notepad just to write "buy milk." 

And as for the tomato plants, well, you really need a full range of motion for those! I grow the indeterminate varieties—Early Girls and some big heirloom Beefsteaks—and they just grow and grow like absolute weeds if you let them. You have to really reach up high to tie them to the stakes, stretching your arms all the way out and around the cages. I use that green stretchy tape, you know the kind I'm talking about? It comes in a little roll. It’s brilliant because it doesn't cut into the stems when the wind blows and the plant gets heavy with fruit.

Usually, her comments are more along the lines of asking me to sit still because I’m shaking the whole couch while we’re trying to watch Jeopardy. I get restless, you know? Especially if the category is something I’m not interested in, like 19th-century opera or pop music from the 2010s. I’ll start bouncing my knee, or I’ll get up to go check if I locked the back door, even though I know I already checked it after dinner. 

So, it's definitely not a matter of moving less or having a hard time moving. I can hop up out of a chair just fine, cross my legs, uncross them—no stiffness, no effort at all. I’m always in motion, really. It’s like I have this excess energy that just has to go somewhere, even if I'm just sitting down reading a book or watching television. So no, nobody has ever told me I seem to move less, and I certainly haven't noticed anything like that myself. I'm just as squirmy as I've always been!

doctor.intent: Distinguish between Parkinson's disease (G30.9) and other medical conditions causing cognitive dysfunction (F06.8) by assessing for the presence of bradykinesia, which is a cardinal feature of Parkinson's disease that the patient may not have spontaneously reported despite denying other motor symptoms.
doctor.question: When you're doing something like buttoning those flannel shirts you mentioned, or writing with your fountain pen, do you ever notice that your movements feel like they're happening in slow motion, or that it takes you longer to complete the movement than you expect, even though you're not trying to go slowly?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about bradykinesia or slow movements, which is not part of my ADHD symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Slow motion? Oh, no, not at all. Actually, it's quite the opposite. I tend to rush through things. Take those flannel shirts, for instance. I love a good flannel, especially this time of year when there's that little bit of a chill in the morning air before the sun really hits the back porch. I have this one absolute favorite—it's a red and black buffalo check, very classic, you know the exact type I mean. I think I got it from a catalog, maybe ten or twelve years ago. The cuffs are getting a little frayed, but the cotton is just perfectly broken in now. 

Anyway, when I'm putting that on in the mornings, I just zip right through the buttons. Zip, zip, zip. In fact, half the time I do it so fast that I get to the bottom and realize I've skipped a button right in the middle, so the two sides of the shirt don't line up at the hem. Then I have to undo the whole thing and start completely over! But that's just because I'm rushing and thinking about what I'm going to make for breakfast, not paying attention to what my hands are actually doing. It's definitely not because my hands are moving slowly. There's absolutely no delay or sluggishness there. 

And the exact same goes for the fountain pen. Like I was saying earlier about that medium nib, if you hover too long or move in slow motion, you’re going to end up with a massive ink blot ruining your paper. The ink just flows too generously for that. You really have to keep the pen moving constantly. I write pretty quickly, probably faster than I should, honestly, because sometimes my brain is three sentences ahead of my hand, and I'm just trying to physically keep up with my own train of thought before I lose it entirely. So my hand is just flying across the page. If anything, I really wish I could force myself to slow down a little bit so my handwriting would be a bit neater, but it never feels like my muscles are moving in slow motion or taking longer than I want them to. Everything fires right on time, at normal speed, or maybe even a little too fast for my own good!

doctor.intent: Determine if patient has experienced delirium (acute confusion with fluctuating consciousness) versus a chronic neurodegenerative condition. The key distinguishing feature would be acute onset with fluctuation. Delirium (F06.8) typically has acute onset and fluctuates, while Parkinson's disease (G30.9) has insidious onset and progressive course. Given the patient denies acute confusion, fluctuation, and hallucinations, and given the 11-month stable course without progression, I need to clarify whether there were ANY acute episodes of confusion or altered mental status in the 11 months since onset, even brief ones, to rule out delirium.
doctor.question: Looking back over these past eleven months since your cousin moved in, has there been any single day or even just a few hours where you suddenly felt like your thinking was really scrambled or confused—where it felt different from your usual forgetfulness—even if it only lasted a short time before you felt better?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about sudden, temporary periods of confusion or scrambled thinking (delirium), which is not part of my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Scrambled or confused? No, no, definitely not. I mean, having my cousin here these past eleven months has certainly been... well, it’s been an adjustment, let’s put it that way. When he first moved in, he brought so much stuff with him. Just boxes and boxes of things he hasn't even looked at since, I don't know, the late nineties probably. Old magazines, random car parts, you name it. It completely threw my routine out the window, and my wife was just pulling her hair out trying to figure out where to put it all without turning our living room into a storage unit. 

So, sure, my usual forgetfulness probably flared up a bit just because my environment was completely upended. Like, if I set my glasses down on a stack of his mail on the kitchen island, I'd completely lose them for half the day. Or I'd walk into the guest room to ask him a question, get distracted by some weird antique lamp he unpacked, and completely forget why I went in there. But that’s just my normal scattered brain, you know? It’s exactly what I've always dealt with. It’s never a sudden wave of actual confusion or feeling disoriented. 

I always know exactly who I am, where I am, and what's going on around me. My mind itself isn't scrambled, it's just... bouncing around between too many things at once because there's extra chaos in the house right now. But no, there hasn't been a single day, or even a few hours, where I felt that kind of sudden, out-of-the-blue confusion you're talking about. It's just the same old me, just with a little more clutter to get distracted by!

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with an 11-month history of progressive memory impairment (difficulty encoding and retaining new information, misplacing objects) and concentration difficulties that began acutely following a significant psychosocial stressor (cousin's move-in requiring increased caregiving demands). Notably absent are cardinal features of neurodegenerative disease: no motor symptoms (tremor, rigidity, bradykinesia, gait disturbance), no facial hypomimia, no reduced arm swing, no bradykinesia, no reduced movement amplitude, and normal fine motor control. Additionally, recent comprehensive medical workup (within past 3 months) was completely normal including labs and vital signs. The cognitive symptoms are non-progressive over the 11-month period and appear situationally reactive rather than showing the inexorable decline expected in Alzheimer's disease. The clinical picture is most consistent with mild neurocognitive disorder due to psychosocial stress (F06.8 - Other specified mental disorder due to known physiological condition), though adjustment disorder with mixed disturbance of emotions and conduct cannot be entirely excluded.
